stem: A 23-year-old woman, gravida 1 para 0, comes to the hospital at 30 weeks gestation with preterm, prelabor rupture of membranes.  Her pregnancy has been complicated by first trimester bleeding due to a subchorionic hemorrhage.  Vital signs are normal.  Pelvic examination shows pooling of clear vaginal discharge consistent with ruptured membranes.  The patient's cervix is visually closed, and she has no uterine contractions.  Betamethasone is administered to the mother.  This medication has which of the following effects on the fetus?​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​​​​​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​
explanation:
Fetal effects due to obstetric medications

Medication

Fetal effects

Corticosteroids(betamethasone, dexamethasone)

  • ↓ Risk of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome
  • Accelerates type 1 & 2 pneumocyte maturation:
    • ↑ Alveolar surfactant
    • ↓ Alveolar surface tension
    • ↑ Lung compliance & maximal lung volume
    • ↓ Pulmonary vascular permeability

Magnesium sulfate

  • ↓ Risk of cerebral palsy (hypoxic-ischemic brain injury), possibly due to:
    • ↓ Cerebral vasoconstriction
    • ↓ Cerebral inflammation
    • ↓ Neuromuscular excitability

Indomethacin

  • ↑ Vasoconstriction (due to ↓ prostaglandin E2 synthesis)
  • ↓ Ductus arteriosus patency (eg, premature closure of the ductus arteriosus)
  • ↓ Renal perfusion & urine output (oligohydramnios)

Premature infants, particularly those delivered at <34 weeks gestation, are at significant risk of respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) due to fetal lung immaturity.  Corticosteroids (eg, betamethasone, dexamethasone) can be administered antenatally to reduce the incidence and severity of RDS and improve neonatal survival.

In the terminal saccular stage of lung development, type 2 pneumocytes begin producing significant amounts of pulmonary surfactant, a lipoprotein complex rich in phospholipids (most notably dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine [DPPC], a type of lecithin).  Surfactant decreases alveolar surface tension by creating a lipid-rich monolayer separating alveolar gas from the underlying aqueous fluid.  Surfactant reduces alveolar opening pressure, increases lung compliance, and prevents end-expiratory atelectasis.

Pulmonary surfactant production (ie, quantity, quality) depends on fetal pneumocyte maturity and improves with increasing gestational age.  Corticosteroids accelerate fetal pneumocyte development; therefore, corticosteroids are administered to mothers at risk for preterm delivery (such as this patient at 30 weeks gestation with preterm, prelabor rupture of membranes) to increase surfactant production and improve neonatal respiratory function.

(Choice B)  Hypoxic-ischemic brain injury and prematurity are risk factors for cerebral palsy (CP).  Antenatal administration of magnesium sulfate (not corticosteroids) can decrease the incidence and severity of CP in premature infants by likely mitigating inflammatory and excitatory injury to fetal neurons.

(Choice C)  The fetal ductus arteriosus (DA) normally closes after birth due to increased oxygen tension and falling prostaglandin levels.  Increased DA patency (ie, a PDA) may be desirable in neonates born with ductal-dependent congenital heart defects (eg, transposition of the great arteries) and can be achieved by administering exogenous prostaglandins (not corticosteroids).  In contrast, cyclooxygenase inhibitors (eg, indomethacin) decrease local prostaglandin production, causing vasoconstriction and premature DA closure.

(Choice D)  Corticosteroids also stimulate type 1 pneumocyte maturation, leading to development of the capillary-alveolar barrier, which optimizes gas exchange, and decreased pulmonary vascular permeability, which discourages fluid leakage into the alveoli so that the fetus can transition to breathing air once delivered.

(Choice E)  Corticosteroids can cause vasoconstriction or vasodilation depending on the vessel type.  Corticosteroids have been shown to vasodilate the placental vessels, including the umbilical artery.

Educational objective:Corticosteroids (eg, betamethasone, dexamethasone) are administered to pregnant women at risk of preterm delivery to prevent neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.  Corticosteroids accelerate fetal lung maturation by stimulating production of surfactant, which decreases alveolar surface tension to improve lung function.​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​​​​​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​
